questions.question: Explain the difference between a number scale and a bar scale, and say why a builder trusts the bar scale on a photocopied plan.
questions.expected_answer: A number scale is a ratio such as 1 : 50, meaning one unit on the drawing stands for fifty of the same units in reality, so on a 1 : 50 plan 1 cm represents 50 cm, or 0,5 m; the units must be identical on both sides of the ratio. A bar scale is a small ruler printed on the drawing itself, divided into segments each labelled with the real distance it represents — on this plan every 2 cm segment stands for 1 m, which is the same relationship as 1 : 50. The ratio is only a promise about the page at its original size, so photocopying at 80 percent or zooming on a phone quietly makes it false. The bar scale is printed on the same page and shrinks or stretches with the drawing, so it stays true at any size — which is why builders measure against the bar and treat the printed ratio as a label.

questions.question: A bedroom measures 9,0 cm by 6,4 cm on a 1 : 50 plan. Find its real dimensions and work out the cost of carpet at R165,00/m² and skirting at R38,00/m, allowing for a 0,9 m doorway.
questions.expected_answer: Going from plan to reality you multiply by the scale: 9,0 × 50 = 450 cm = 4,50 m, and 6,4 × 50 = 320 cm = 3,20 m, with the unit written on every line. Carpet covers the floor, so it needs AREA: 4,50 × 3,20 = 14,4 m², and 14,4 × R165,00 = R2 376,00. Skirting runs around the edge of the floor, so it needs PERIMETER, not area: 2 × (4,50 + 3,20) = 15,4 m. No skirting crosses the doorway, so subtract 0,9 m to get 14,5 m, and 14,5 × R38,00 = R551,00. Choosing area for the carpet and perimeter for the skirting is the decision the marks are really testing.

questions.question: State what a floor plan shows that an elevation cannot, and what an elevation shows that a floor plan cannot. Then use both to find the wall area of the new room.
questions.expected_answer: A floor plan is the view from directly above with the roof lifted away, so it shows layout: the arrangement of rooms, floor areas, wall thicknesses, where doors and windows sit along a wall, and how the spaces connect. An elevation is a straight-on view of one side with no perspective, so it shows heights: the wall height, the shape and pitch of the roof, how far above the floor the window sill sits, steps and gutters. Neither drawing is complete on its own, and combining them is what a full question requires. The floor plan gives the perimeter, 2 × (4,50 + 3,20) = 15,4 m, and the elevation gives the wall height, 2,6 m, so the wall surface is 15,4 × 2,6 = 40,04 m². Subtracting the door (0,9 × 2,1 = 1,89 m²) and the window (1,5 × 1,0 = 1,5 m²) leaves 36,65 m² of wall to be plastered or painted.
